title: SaddlePoint POC weekly — throughput profiling & triage
next_steps: Redwood to run controlled 10k-concurrency stress with KV cache enabled and share annotated results & logs by 2027-06-10
Customer to export production traces for the peak 95th percentile windows (last 7 days) and share via secure link by 2027-06-09
Schedule on-prem pilot kickoff (network/VPC config checklist) — target 2027-06-15
Redwood SE to propose adjusted batching profile (min_batch_ms + adaptive window) and recommended concurrency targets by 2027-06-11
action_items: Maya Chen — send updated benchmark spreadsheet and annotated runbook with column descriptions by 2027-06-10
Diego Alvarez — run KV-enabled stress test + include per-GPU metrics (util, mem, kernel stalls) by 2027-06-10
Tomoko Saito — provide live traces and sample request distribution (payload sizes, token lengths) by 2027-06-09
Jared Patel — confirm internal decision criteria for Dedicated vs Private (cost vs SLA) by 2027-06-14
summary: Weekly POC sync to triage throughput bottlenecks. Main observations: KV/prefix caching reduces tokens/sec variability but increases tail latency in some bursts; continuous batching parameters need tightening (min_batch_ms and max_batch_size); concurrency target of 600 concurrent streams on A100 equivalent yields best cost/latency tradeoff in our runs; queueing backpressure observed when request size variance is high. Agreed next steps: run a targeted 10k-concurrency stress with KV cache on, customer to share traces, and plan on-prem kickoff for mid-June.
transcript:
Header: 2027-06-08 10:30Z | Duration ~50m | Redwood: Maya Chen, Diego Alvarez | SaddlePoint: Jared Patel, Lena Morris, Tomoko Saito, Amir Khan

[00:00] Maya (AE): okay great thanks everyone for jumping on, quick agenda — run through last week's runs, call out hotspots, propose a retune and agree next steps. Is that ok on time?
[00:15] Jared: yep that's good. we've been seeing the same mid-day spike around 11:30 UTC so hopefully we can pin that down.
[00:22] Diego (SE): quick note, I pulled the last three nightly runs and put them in the spreadsheet Maya shared, you should see per-shard GPU util, kernel errors, and the tokens per second curve. there are some interesting shapes when KV cache is toggled.
[00:35] Lena: yeah we saw pretty consistent throughput increases with KV but also a weird tail at like the 95/99th percentiles where some requests jumped to +200ms.
[00:44] Speaker 1: (inaudible) that was on the H1 00 machines?
[00:48] Diego (SE): so there are two factors — when the prefix cache hits, we reduce infer-time per token but we sometimes increase branching in the runtime for cache lookup and remote fetch; on small payloads that's great, on variable-length payloads with lots of concurrency it can create transient stalls.
[01:05] Amir: right, our payload distribution is heavy-tailed — a lot of short requests but some mega prompts for aggregation jobs.
[01:12] Maya (AE): can you remind us of the current concurrency target in the POC config? I thought we were at 400?
[01:18] Diego (SE): current client concurrency target is 400, queue depth cap of 200 per-shard, continuous batch min_batch_ms 6, max_batch_size 48. we tested a run at 600 concurrency last night and saw better avg throughput but tail got worse if KV was enabled.
[01:36] Lena: curious — was that 600 across the fleet or per-pool?
[01:40] Diego (SE): across the test pool, roughly equivalent to 3 A100s in our env. the per-GPU concurrency was still within limits, but queueing jitter increased.
[01:51] Jared: so is this more of a batching window issue or an orchestration/routing problem?
[01:56] Diego (SE): leaning toward batching window plus request-size variance. continuous batching helps smooth throughput but if min_batch_ms is too high you add latency; too low and you starve the GPU from large sustained batches. when KV hits and returns variable sized prefixes, the batch packing becomes uneven.
[02:15] Maya (AE): ok let's try to be concrete — what's the narrow set of parameters to adjust this week?
[02:20] Diego (SE): propose: reduce min_batch_ms to 3, keep max_batch_size at 48, enable adaptive windowing that increases min_batch_ms under burst detection, and add a small prefix-cache grace TTL to avoid excessive lookups for the same key in tight windows. run that at concurrency 600 and 1000 for comparison.
[02:38] Tomoko: how do we capture per-request queue time and attribution? our current traces are pretty coarse.
[02:45] Diego (SE): we can instrument a short-latency tracer on the client -> router path we use; I'll add per-hop timestamps and an aggregated histogram for queue times. need two things from you: request distribution and a sample of the largest prompts.
[02:58] Tomoko: ok will share.
[03:02] Jared: also remind me — are you running quantized models for some of these runs? we heard mention of quantizashun a few calls ago and wanted to understand cost effects.
[03:11] Maya (AE): yes we did a quantized run (int8) vs fp16 baseline. quantization helped cost but slightly increased per-token variance on long sequences. Diego can speak to kernel selection.
[03:21] Diego (SE): kernel choice matters; quantized kernels on H100-like hardware performed well for steady loads but had higher stalls during reshuffle. that's expected — the kernel path for quant needs slightly different memory access patterns.
[03:32] Lena: ok, on the spreadsheets, which run had the prefix TTL? I may have missed that column.
[03:37] Diego (SE): column `prefix_ttl_ms` — last night's 600-run had it off. I'll mark runs with TTL turned on in the next upload.
[03:44] Speaker 2 (low audio): can you also test reduced batch sizes?
[03:47] Diego (SE): yes we'll include a 24 max batch size run as part of the matrix.
[03:50] Maya (AE): let's talk about fallbacks — if we hit a sustained surge, what's the recommended approach? Dedicated bursts vs fallback to a smaller/cheaper model?
[03:59] Jared: we prefer fallback to smaller model if quality is acceptable, because Dedicated reservation bumping is expensive for us.
[04:06] Diego (SE): fair — Redwood supports automatic routing to compatible variants. plan would be: keep primary on verified LLM, have a lighter quantized variant for burst fallback, and configure a latency SLO tier that triggers the fallback at 95th p95 > 220ms for 60s.
[04:24] Amir: can we set different thresholds for read-only endpoints vs full-generation?
[04:29] Maya (AE): yes routing policies can be per-route. we'll capture that use case.
[04:33] Lena: a quick data point — our production median token length is 18 but the top 3% are 600+ tokens, which is driving the heavy tail.
[04:41] Diego (SE): that explains the tail behaviors. continuous batching is great when token-length distribution is narrow; with heavy tails you either isolate long-running requests to a separate pool or accept higher tail latency.
[04:55] Jared: let's consider a dedicated long-request pool then, to preserve short-request latency. cost tradeoff?
[05:01] Maya (AE): we can model cost in the spreadsheet — Diego can sketch expected tokens/sec per-pool and cost/hour with current committed capacity assumptions.
[05:09] Diego (SE): noted — I'll add a scenario page: short-pool (low latency) vs long-pool (high throughput) and hybrid with dynamic routing.
[05:18] Maya (AE): any security or VPC notes before we plan the on-prem kickoff?
[05:22] Tomoko: we need the KMS/HSM spec and audit log retention details. also SSO/SAML integration checklist.
[05:29] Maya (AE): we'll share the security pack — SOC2 checklist, KMS pattern, RBAC examples. add to next steps.
[05:36] Speaker 3: (crosstalk about file links)
[05:40] Diego (SE): quick housekeeping — because traces are sensitive, use the secure link we dropped in the deck, don't upload to public s3.
[05:46] Lena: noted.
[05:48] Maya (AE): recap time — Diego, what are you running this week?
[05:51] Diego (SE): matrix: concurrency [400, 600, 1000], prefix_ttl [off, 30ms, 100ms], min_batch_ms [3,6], max_batch_size [24,48], quantized [on, off]. will run the 10k-concurrency stress with KV on in a controlled env and capture per-GPU kernel metrics.
[06:08] Maya (AE): Tomoko to send request distribution and large prompt samples by 2027-06-09; Diego to share annotated runs by 2027-06-10; Maya to send security pack + updated spreadsheet by 2027-06-10; Jared to confirm Dedicated vs Private decision criteria by 2027-06-14.
[06:22] Jared: sounds good. one more question — competitors, we saw FastServe's recent benchmark claiming p50 18ms but no tail data, is that relevant?
[06:31] Diego (SE): we noted that but their tests looked synthetic; we'll focus on real traces.
[06:36] Amir: any quick wins we can do now? like client-side rate shaping?
[06:40] Diego (SE): yes client-side leaky-bucket to smooth bursts helps; also small request-side timeout/retry logic to avoid pile-up. we'll propose recommended client params.
[06:51] Lena: thanks all.
[06:53] Maya (AE): great — we'll follow up in the channel with the links. thanks everyone.
[07:00] (end)

Notes: Some speaker labels were noisy — occasional Speaker 1/2; some words mis-transcribed (quantizashun, Kubermates seen in earlier notes). Attach: benchmark_spreadsheet_v3.xlsx (link in meeting chat), secure-trace-upload-instructions.md (link).
